Editorial rewrite of advisor and client prose; substance unchanged.
Added the §274(o) carve-out: occasional overtime meal money remains 50% deductible after 2025 as a de minimis fringe.

advisor.summary: Section 132(e) excludes from an employee's income property or services so small in value, and provided so infrequently, that accounting for them is administratively impracticable — occasional snacks, group meals, modest holiday gifts of property, flowers marking life events. Properly classified, these items remain deductible to the employer, tax-free to the employee, and off payroll altogether. Two hard edges cause nearly every failure in practice: cash and gift cards are never de minimis at any amount, and frequency is half the test — a routine perk is wages. Employer-provided phones travel under their own safe harbor, Notice 2011-72. The 2026 change is deduction-side: §274(o) denies the employer deduction for eating-facility and convenience-of-the-employer meal costs paid after 2025, so on-site meal programs keep the employee exclusion but lose the write-off.
mechanics: The §132(e)(1) test weighs value and frequency together: a small item given occasionally is excludable, while the identical item given routinely fails, because frequency makes accounting practicable — and no statutory dollar threshold offers cover.

Under Reg. §1.132-6(c), cash and cash equivalents — gift cards and general-purpose certificates — are taxable wages at any amount; the lone exception is occasional meal money or cab fare for overtime work, and 'occasional' does all the work.

Employer-provided cell phones carry a separate safe harbor: under Notice 2011-72, a phone furnished for noncompensatory business reasons is a working-condition fringe, its personal use is de minimis, and no usage logs are required.

The regulations' own examples set the category's scale — occasional parties and picnics, low-value holiday gifts of property, coffee and doughnuts, occasional supper money: small, irregular, impractical to track.

For amounts paid after December 31, 2025, §274(o) denies the employer deduction for eating-facility and §119 convenience meals; the employee-side §132(e) exclusion survives, but the employer economics of on-site meal programs have changed — occasional overtime meal money, by contrast, keeps a 50% deduction because it is a de minimis fringe rather than a §119 convenience meal.

authority.note: The exclusion itself and its impracticability standard — value and frequency weighed as one test.
The operative rules and examples; subsection (c) states the absolute bar on cash and gift cards.
The employer cell-phone safe harbor: business-reason phones are excludable, personal use is de minimis, and no records are required.
The 2026 disallowance of the employer deduction for eating facilities and convenience-of-the-employer meals.

requirements: Perks that are genuinely small and genuinely occasional — frequency carries half the test.
A written policy that lists the perks offered and states the no-cash, no-gift-card rule.
Payroll coordination: anything cash-like lands on the W-2; qualifying items never touch it.
For phones, a documented noncompensatory business reason — a single memo covers the program.
risks: Gift cards are the universal exam finding: wages at any amount, and a payroll audit reclassifies them across every employee and every open year, with back taxes and penalties — the cleanup always costs more than the policy would have.
Frequency creep turns perks into compensation — daily meal money or a standing monthly gift fails even at trivial dollar amounts.
No safe-harbor dollar amount exists; an adviser quoting a fixed figure is estimating, not citing.
Perks that flow mainly to owners read as disguised distributions, not fringe benefits.
On-site meal programs lose the employer deduction in 2026 under §274(o) — clients budgeting on the old treatment will overstate the write-off.
stateNotes: Conformity: states that start from federal AGI or federal taxable income conform to the §132(e) exclusion automatically — properly classified perks never reach the state base.
PTET interaction: perk costs are ordinary entity deductions that already reduce the base of any pass-through entity tax election; no separate PTET step is needed.
Missouri: conforms through its federal starting point (RSMo §143.121), with no fringe-benefit addback.
reviewChecklist: Perk inventory complete, with each item classified: de minimis, working-condition, taxable wage, or 2026 deduction-limited meals.
Written fringe policy adopted, with the no-cash rule and frequency guardrails.
Gift-card practices stopped or deliberately run through payroll as bonuses.
Phone-program business-reason memo in the file.

client.teaser: The small perks you already give your team can stay off everyone's tax forms.
client.headline: Keep the small stuff tax-free — for your business and your team
plainEnglish: The tax law has a common-sense rule. Perks too small to be worth tracking are not taxable pay. Coffee and snacks, an occasional team lunch, flowers for a new baby, a modest holiday gift — the business deducts them, the employee owes nothing, and nothing shows up on a W-2.

There are two tripwires. Cash and gift cards never qualify. A $20 gift card is taxable pay, no matter the occasion. And 'occasional' matters — give the same perk all the time and it becomes taxable pay.
Most businesses trip one of these without knowing it. The problem surfaces in a payroll audit, multiplied across every employee and every year. A simple one-page policy stops it before it starts.
client.analogy: It is like the express lane at the store. Small and occasional sails right through. Push a full cart in, and the whole load gets pulled aside.
benefits: Team perks that cost less than a matching raise would
Nothing added to W-2s, and no payroll tax
Company phones handled cleanly with a single memo
Protection from the gift-card mistake most businesses make
steps: WE review the perks you give now and flag anything mislabeled.
WE write a one-page policy with the do's and don'ts.
YOU follow the policy — real items, given now and then, never cash or cards.
WE check in each year to keep the program clean.
clientCommitments: No cash or gift cards as perks — run those through payroll instead
Keep perks occasional, and tell us before any perk becomes routine

annualMaintenance: Yearly perk-inventory review to catch frequency creep and mislabeled items
Year-end check that payroll captured any gifts that did not qualify
deliverables: Business-purpose memo for the phone program
